title: Roaming Pricing Structure by Region
content: Roaming charges are tiered by region rather than by individual country. Zone A covers North America and Western Europe and bills at the customer's standard per-MB data rate with no surcharge on voice calls. Zone B covers Eastern Europe, parts of Asia-Pacific, and Latin America, and applies a 1.5x multiplier to standard voice and SMS rates, with data billed per 10MB block rather than continuously. Zone C, covering all remaining destinations, uses a flat daily pass model: customers are charged a fixed daily fee once any roaming activity is detected, capping their total exposure for that day regardless of usage volume. Customers on the Unlimited Plus and Premium Unlimited plans receive Zone A roaming at no additional charge; all other plans are billed per the zone table above. Consultants should confirm the customer's destination zone before quoting a rate, since the same country can occasionally shift zones during promotional periods. Roaming charge disputes are only eligible for refund if filed within 30 days of the statement date on which the charge appeared — see the billing dispute resolution timeline article for the full process. When a customer disputes a roaming charge outside this window, explain the policy plainly rather than escalating, since escalation will not change the outcome.

title: Data Rollover Policy
content: Unused data from a billing cycle rolls over to the following cycle only, and only for postpaid plans of 10GB or larger. Rolled-over data is consumed before the customer's fresh monthly allowance, and any rollover balance not used within that single following cycle is forfeited — it does not accumulate further. Prepaid plans and plans under 10GB do not support rollover in any form; unused data on those plans expires at the end of the billing cycle with no exception. Family Share plans pool rollover across all lines on the account rather than tracking it per line, which occasionally causes confusion when one family member expects to see their own individual rollover balance. When explaining this to a customer, clarify that the pooled amount is shared and any line can draw from it. Rollover data never counts against a customer's contractual data cap for purposes of overage billing — it is treated as already-paid-for capacity being used later, not new usage. If a customer's rollover balance appears to be missing entirely, the most common cause is a plan change mid-cycle, which resets rollover eligibility; check the plan change history before treating this as a system error.

title: Family Plan Rules and Member Limits
content: A Family Share plan supports between 2 and 6 lines under a single primary account holder, who is the only person authorized to add or remove lines, change the shared data allowance, or update the payment method for the group. Each additional line beyond the second carries a flat per-line fee, discounted progressively as more lines are added, with the steepest discount applying to the fifth and sixth lines. All lines share one data pool as described in the data rollover policy article, but each line retains its own voice minutes and SMS allowance, which are not shared. A secondary line holder can request account information about their own line but cannot authorize changes to the plan structure or billing — any such request must be redirected to the primary account holder. If a secondary line holder insists on making a plan-level change, do not process it; explain that only the primary holder can authorize it, and offer to note the request for when the primary holder next contacts support. Removing a line from a Family Share plan does not prorate that month's shared charge — the fee structure is fixed for the billing cycle in which the removal occurs and adjusts starting the following cycle.

title: Device Trade-In Program Overview
content: The device trade-in program credits customers toward a new device purchase based on the condition and model of their traded-in device, assessed against a standard valuation table updated quarterly. Devices are graded as Excellent, Good, Fair, or Not Eligible; a cracked screen or non-functional camera automatically caps a device at Fair grade regardless of other condition factors. Trade-in credit is applied as a bill credit spread over the length of the new device's installment plan, not as an immediate cash-equivalent discount, and is forfeited if the customer cancels service before the installment plan completes. A device that fails to power on can still be traded in, but only at a fixed low-value tier separate from the standard grading table, since functional condition cannot be verified. Consultants should never quote an exact trade-in value over the phone — the final value is only confirmed once the device is physically inspected at a store or through the mail-in kit. Provide the customer with the estimated range from the valuation table and clearly state that it is an estimate, not a guarantee, to avoid disputes later if the device grades lower than expected upon inspection.

title: Early Termination Fees and Waivers
content: Contracts under a 24-month term carry an early termination fee that decreases linearly each month the contract has been active, reaching zero once the full term is served. The fee is calculated from the device subsidy remaining, not a flat penalty, so two customers cancelling in the same month can owe different amounts depending on which device they financed. A waiver of this fee is available automatically once a customer has reached 24 months of tenure, since at that point they are considered to have fulfilled the spirit of the original agreement even if a newer contract term is still technically active from a renewal. Waivers requested before the 24-month tenure mark are not automatic and require explicit supervisor approval as a goodwill exception — these should be reserved for cases involving service failures attributable to the company, not simple customer preference to switch providers. When a customer requests a waiver and does not meet the tenure threshold, do not imply a waiver is likely; state that it requires supervisor review and that approval is not guaranteed. Document the reason for the cancellation request regardless of outcome, since this data feeds into retention program design.

title: SIM Replacement Process and Fees
content: A standard SIM replacement fee applies whenever a customer requests a new SIM card, whether due to physical damage, loss, or a form-factor change (such as moving from a standard SIM to an eSIM). The fee is waived automatically for the first replacement request within any rolling 12-month window; a second request inside that same window requires the standard fee unless a supervisor explicitly approves a waiver. The replacement window resets on a rolling basis from the date of the most recent replacement, not on a fixed calendar schedule, so consultants should check the account's SIM replacement history rather than assuming based on calendar year. A blocked or not-activated SIM status does not, by itself, indicate a replacement is needed — many such cases resolve through reactivation or a device restart rather than a physical swap. Only issue a replacement once activation and device-side troubleshooting have been ruled out, since an unnecessary replacement still counts against the customer's 12-month fee-waiver window. New SIM cards are typically active within 15 minutes of activation confirmation for physical SIMs, and near-instantly for eSIM QR provisioning, so set customer expectations accordingly rather than quoting a multi-hour delay.

title: Prepaid vs Postpaid Plan Differences
content: Prepaid plans require payment in advance of service and do not support billing disputes in the traditional sense, since there is no invoice to dispute — any concern about a prepaid balance deduction is handled as a usage inquiry rather than a billing dispute. Postpaid plans bill in arrears for the prior month's usage plus the upcoming month's base plan fee, and are the only plan type eligible for the standard billing dispute and refund process. Prepaid customers cannot roll over unused balance beyond the validity period printed on their plan (typically 30 days), while postpaid customers are subject to the separate data rollover policy for unused data specifically, not for unused minutes or credit. Switching from postpaid to prepaid requires the postpaid account to be paid in full and closed first — it is a full account type change, not a plan change, and cannot be reversed same-day. Prepaid accounts do not support Family Share plans; each prepaid line is independent with its own balance and no pooled resources. When a prepaid customer's balance reaches zero, service is suspended immediately rather than continuing with an outstanding balance, which is the core structural difference consultants should lead with when explaining plan type to a confused customer.

title: International Calling Rates
content: International calling rates (calls made from a domestic connection to a foreign number, distinct from roaming charges incurred while physically abroad) are billed per minute according to a destination-country rate card that is separate from the roaming zone table. Most plans include a small allowance of international minutes to a defined list of common destinations; calls beyond that allowance, or to destinations not on the list, are billed at the standard per-minute rate for that country. Some premium plans include unlimited international calling to a fixed set of 15 countries, which is a plan feature distinct from any roaming benefit and remains active even when the customer is roaming abroad and calling back home. Rates are highest for satellite phone numbers, premium-rate international numbers, and a small list of sanctioned or restricted destinations, which may be blocked entirely rather than merely expensive. When a customer disputes an international calling charge, first confirm whether the call was placed from a domestic connection (international calling) or while abroad (roaming) — the two have entirely separate billing rules and rate cards, and misidentifying which applies is a common source of consultant error when explaining the charge.

title: Device Warranty Claims Process
content: Devices purchased through the company carry the manufacturer's standard warranty (typically 12 months) plus an optional extended protection plan customers may purchase separately. A warranty claim for a manufacturing defect is handled at no cost to the customer provided the device shows no signs of physical damage, liquid exposure, or unauthorized repair attempts, any of which void the warranty regardless of the original defect. Before referring a customer to a repair center, consultants must confirm the device is still within its warranty or protection plan window, since promising a free repair outside that window creates an unfunded commitment the repair center will not honor. Devices without an active warranty or protection plan can still be referred for paid out-of-warranty repair, but this must be stated clearly as a paid service, not implied to be free. Loaner devices are available during repair only for customers on the extended protection plan, not for standard warranty claims. If a device fails multiple times for the same defect within the warranty period, escalate for a replacement rather than a further repair, since repeated repair attempts on the same issue is itself grounds for replacement under the manufacturer's lemon-device policy.

title: Loyalty Program Tiers and Benefits
content: The loyalty program has three tenure-based tiers: Silver (12-23 months), Gold (24-47 months), and Platinum (48+ months), with benefits increasing at each tier. Silver tier includes priority queue placement when contacting support. Gold tier adds eligibility for a loyalty discount on the monthly plan cost, capped at 15% regardless of how long the customer has held Gold status. Platinum tier adds the Gold benefits plus one free device upgrade every 24 months independent of the standard device installment cycle. The 15% discount cap at Gold and Platinum tiers is a hard ceiling — it cannot be increased by a supervisor override, unlike some other policy exceptions in this handbook, because it is enforced as a system-level billing rule rather than a discretionary consultant action. Tenure is calculated from the original account opening date and is not reset by plan changes, device upgrades, or temporary suspensions, but is reset if the account is fully closed and later reopened as a new account. When a customer asks why their discount did not apply, first confirm their actual tier eligibility date before assuming a system error, since a common cause is the customer miscounting their own tenure by a few months around a tier boundary.

title: Data Privacy Policy for Consultants
content: Consultants may only access and discuss account information for the verified account holder of the account they are currently working on. Identity verification (security questions, or another approved method) must succeed before any account-specific detail is shared, including balance, plan details, device information, or ticket history — this applies even if the caller claims to be a family member or claims urgency. A secondary line holder on a Family Share plan may only access information about their own line, not the primary holder's billing details or other lines on the account, per the family plan rules article. Under no circumstances should a consultant look up or discuss an account other than the one the current verified caller is authorized for, even out of curiosity or to cross-reference a similar-sounding issue — this is treated as a serious policy violation regardless of intent. If a caller cannot pass identity verification, do not disclose any account information, including confirming whether an account exists at all for a given name or number; state only that verification could not be completed and offer the standard alternative verification path. Any suspected attempt at social engineering (a caller probing for information without being able to verify) should be logged and escalated per the fraud detection process, not simply declined and forgotten.

title: Fraud Detection and Escalation Process
content: Suspicious payment activity includes repeated failed payment attempts using different payment methods in a short window, a sudden change of payment method immediately followed by a high-value purchase or plan upgrade, or account access from a device or region inconsistent with the account's established pattern. When any of these indicators are present, escalate to the fraud team immediately rather than continuing standard troubleshooting, since further account changes during a suspected fraud event can compound the exposure. Every fraud escalation must be logged with a case ID within one hour of the escalation being raised — this is a hard compliance requirement, not a best-practice suggestion, and delayed logging is itself treated as a process failure during audits. While a fraud case is open, do not process any billing changes, plan changes, or password resets on the affected account, even if the caller passes standard identity verification, since the verification method itself may be compromised in an active fraud scenario. Once the fraud team closes a case, they will provide explicit written clearance before the account resumes normal servicing; consultants should not resume normal handling based on the customer's assurance that the issue is resolved. False positives are expected and acceptable — escalating a case that turns out to be legitimate customer behavior carries far less risk than failing to escalate a genuine fraud event.

title: Billing Dispute Resolution Timeline
content: A billing dispute must be filed within 90 days of the statement date on which the disputed charge appeared; disputes filed after this window are not eligible for refund regardless of the charge's validity, since billing records beyond this period are archived and no longer available for verification in the standard support system. Within the 90-day window, disputes under $50 can be resolved and refunded directly by the consultant handling the case. Disputes of $50 or more require supervisor approval before the refund is issued, regardless of how clear-cut the dispute appears — this is a hard approval gate, not a suggestion for complex cases only. Roaming-specific charge disputes have a shorter 30-day window rather than the standard 90 days, due to the more time-sensitive nature of verifying roaming carrier records; see the roaming pricing article for details. When a dispute is denied for being outside the window, explain the specific date boundary clearly using the customer's own statement date, since vague explanations of "too old" tend to prolong the call without resolving the customer's underlying frustration. Document every dispute outcome, approved or denied, since dispute patterns per customer inform account-level fraud and churn-risk signals reviewed separately from individual case handling.

title: Outage Service Credit Policy
content: Customers affected by a confirmed network outage in their service area are eligible for a service credit proportional to the duration of the outage, capped at the equivalent of one full billing cycle's charges regardless of how long the outage actually lasted. Credit eligibility requires the outage to be confirmed by network operations as affecting the customer's specific service area — a single customer's individual connectivity issue, without a broader confirmed outage, does not qualify for this credit and should instead be routed through standard device or account troubleshooting. Once network operations confirms an outage, affected accounts in that area are typically credited automatically within the following billing cycle; a consultant does not need to manually calculate and apply the credit unless the automatic process has demonstrably failed for a specific account. When a customer requests a credit for an outage that network operations has not yet confirmed, escalate to network operations for confirmation rather than promising or denying the credit outright, since confirming a real but not-yet-logged outage is common during the early hours of a network incident. Repeated outage credit requests from the same account without a corresponding confirmed outage may indicate a device or account-specific issue masquerading as a network complaint, and should be investigated accordingly.

title: Account Suspension and Reactivation Rules
content: An account is automatically suspended after a payment failure is not resolved within a defined grace period following the failed attempt, during which service continues but the customer receives repeated notices to update payment or clear the balance. Once suspended, the account cannot be reactivated until the full outstanding balance is paid — this is a hard block with no discretionary exception available to consultants, unlike many other policy points in this handbook, since it is enforced at the billing system level. Partial payment does not lift a suspension, even if the partial amount is substantial; the full balance must clear before reactivation processes. Reactivation is typically immediate once payment is confirmed as cleared (not merely submitted), which for some payment methods such as bank transfer can take one to three business days to actually clear even though the customer sees it as submitted immediately. Set this expectation clearly when a customer pays via bank transfer and expects instant reactivation. An account suspended for reasons other than non-payment (such as a fraud hold) follows a different reactivation path entirely and is not resolved by payment — check the specific suspension reason on the account before assuming a billing-only cause.

title: Password Reset and Identity Verification
content: A password reset can only be issued after the caller successfully passes identity verification via the standard security-question method or an approved alternative; this requirement has no exception, including for callers who present as distressed, urgent, or claiming to be the account holder's family member. Once verification succeeds, the reset is delivered via SMS to the phone number on file, not via email or read aloud over the phone, to reduce the risk of an intercepted reset reaching the wrong party. If the phone number on file is itself inaccessible to the caller (a lost or stolen device, for example), a password reset cannot be issued through the standard SMS path, and the caller must instead be routed to an in-person or extended-verification path, since sending the reset by an alternate channel undermines the verification step. Consultants should never read out or otherwise state the existing password, security answers, or any other authentication detail, even to a verified caller, since the standard process never requires a consultant to know or view these values in the first place — if a system displays such a value in plaintext, that is a system defect to report, not a value to share. Every password reset action, successful or attempted, is logged automatically and reviewed periodically for unusual patterns, such as repeated reset requests on the same account in a short window.

title: Roaming Activation Requirements
content: Roaming must be explicitly enabled on an account before it will function, even on plans that include roaming benefits at no extra charge — the benefit determines the price, not whether the feature is switched on. Activation typically takes effect within 10 minutes but can take up to several hours in rare cases involving certain international carrier partners, so set expectations accordingly rather than promising instant activation in every case. A customer whose plan is inactive or pending cannot have roaming activated even if the roaming flag itself is toggled on, since the underlying plan state blocks all service features, roaming included — always confirm plan status first when troubleshooting a roaming activation failure. Device compatibility is a separate requirement from account-level roaming activation: a fully activated roaming feature will still fail to provide service if the customer's device does not support the frequency bands used by carrier partners in the destination country. When both account activation and device compatibility check out but the customer still reports no service abroad, the most likely remaining cause is a temporary partner-carrier network issue in that specific destination, which should be escalated rather than re-checked repeatedly on the same two factors.

title: Device Roaming Compatibility Bands Explained
content: Roaming compatibility depends on whether a device supports the specific radio frequency bands used by partner carriers in the destination country, which is a hardware characteristic set at manufacture and cannot be changed by any account-side setting or software update. Devices sold directly through the company are guaranteed compatible with all current roaming partner regions at time of sale, but older devices, or devices brought from another carrier, may lack support for bands used in certain regions, most commonly parts of Asia-Pacific and South America. A device being "unlocked" (not tied to a specific carrier) is unrelated to roaming band compatibility — an unlocked device can still lack the necessary hardware bands, and a locked device from the company can still be fully compatible. When a customer reports no roaming service despite an active roaming feature and active plan, check the specific device model against the current compatibility list rather than assuming compatibility based on the device being relatively new, since some recent budget-tier devices omit certain international bands to reduce cost. If a device is confirmed incompatible, there is no account-side fix; the only paths forward are borrowing or purchasing a compatible device for the trip, or accepting reduced/no service in that specific region.

title: Refund Approval Thresholds
content: Refunds under $50 fall within a consultant's own authority to approve and issue directly, without requiring a supervisor's sign-off, provided the underlying dispute is otherwise valid per the billing dispute resolution timeline. Refunds of $50 or more always require supervisor approval before issuance, regardless of how clearly justified the refund appears to the consultant handling the case — this threshold is a fixed dollar amount, not a percentage of the customer's bill, so a $50 refund on a $40 plan and a $50 refund on a $200 plan are treated identically. When a refund request is just under the threshold but a consultant is tempted to round up as a goodwill gesture, remember that doing so would push the refund into supervisor-approval territory, so any amount at or above $50 must go through that process regardless of the reason for the extra amount. Supervisor approval should be requested with the dispute details already documented, not as a verbal summary, so the supervisor can review the same information the consultant used to reach their recommendation. A denied supervisor approval should be communicated to the customer as a policy outcome, not attributed to the individual supervisor by name, to keep the conversation focused on policy rather than personalities.

title: Tier 2 Escalation Guidelines
content: A Tier 2 escalation should only be raised once the standard troubleshooting steps available to a Tier 1 consultant have been exhausted for the issue at hand — escalating before attempting the documented standard checks slows resolution overall, since Tier 2 will typically send the case back for those checks to be completed first. Every escalation must include a written summary of the steps already attempted and their outcomes; an escalation without this summary is considered incomplete and may be bounced back to Tier 1 regardless of how urgent the underlying issue is. This requirement exists because Tier 2 handles a high volume of cases and cannot efficiently re-derive troubleshooting history from raw account logs alone. When escalating, note the specific condition or check that ultimately triggered the escalation (for example, "device confirmed roaming-incompatible, no fix available at Tier 1"), since this helps Tier 2 immediately understand the failure point rather than starting from scratch. Escalations related to a suspected fraud event follow a separate, faster path directly to the fraud team rather than general Tier 2, and should not be routed through standard Tier 2 escalation channels — see the fraud detection article for that specific process.

title: Contract Cancellation Process
content: Cancelling a contract before its term completes triggers the early termination fee calculation described in the early termination fees article, unless the customer qualifies for an automatic waiver at 24+ months tenure or receives a discretionary goodwill waiver approved by a supervisor. Before processing any cancellation, confirm the account has no outstanding balance, since an unpaid balance does not block cancellation itself but will still be owed and collected after the account closes, which is a common source of customer confusion and later disputes. Cancellation is effective at the end of the current billing cycle, not immediately upon request, and the customer retains full service access until that cycle ends — do not disable service early even if the customer requests it, since they have already paid for that period. Devices still under an installment plan at the time of cancellation have their remaining balance due immediately as a lump sum, separate from any early termination fee, since the device financing agreement is independent of the service contract. Once a cancellation is processed, it cannot be reversed by simply calling back within the same day — a full new account setup would be required, so confirm the customer's intent clearly before finalizing.

title: SIM Card Activation Timeline
content: A physical SIM card typically activates within 15 minutes of the activation request being submitted, though this can occasionally extend to a few hours during high-volume periods such as major device launch days. An eSIM activated via QR code or carrier app is generally near-instantaneous, since it does not depend on the same physical network provisioning steps as a traditional SIM swap. A SIM showing as "not activated" well beyond the expected window most commonly indicates the activation request itself failed to submit correctly rather than a delay in processing — check the account's activation request log for an actual pending request before assuming a simple delay. New account activations (as opposed to a SIM replacement on an existing account) can take longer, up to 24 hours in some cases, since they also involve provisioning the account itself alongside the SIM. If a customer's SIM remains inactive well past the expected window and a valid activation request is confirmed on file, this should be treated as a technical issue and escalated rather than repeatedly asking the customer to wait longer, since further waiting will not resolve a genuinely stuck provisioning request.

title: Payment Method Update Process
content: Customers can update their payment method at any time, and the new method takes effect for the next scheduled charge; it does not retroactively apply to the current cycle's already-attempted charge. If a payment attempt has already failed using the old method, updating to a new method does not automatically retry the failed charge — the consultant or an automated retry system must explicitly trigger a new attempt using the updated method. Bank transfer payments take one to three business days to clear, which matters directly for account reactivation timing, since reactivation requires the payment to be confirmed cleared, not merely submitted. Credit card and prepaid method updates typically process and clear within minutes. When a customer switches from postpaid billing to a prepaid payment method, clarify that this does not change their plan type (postpaid vs prepaid plan) — payment method and plan type are handled as separate settings, and confusing the two with the customer leads to setting incorrect expectations about billing cycles. Removing a payment method entirely without adding a replacement is not permitted while the account carries an active postpaid plan, since a valid payment method must remain on file at all times for such accounts.

title: Data Plan Upgrade Guidelines
content: A consultant may offer a customer a data plan upgrade of up to one billing tier above their current plan without requiring manager approval; anything beyond one tier above requires manager sign-off, regardless of how strongly the upgrade seems justified by the customer's usage pattern. This limit exists to keep upgrade offers consistent and prevent large, inconsistent jumps in monthly commitment being offered ad hoc across different consultants. Plan upgrades take effect either immediately or at the start of the next billing cycle, depending on the customer's preference, and the consultant should always ask which the customer wants rather than defaulting to one option, since immediate upgrades typically prorate the difference in cost for the remainder of the current cycle. A customer with a pattern of recurring data overage charges is a strong candidate for a proactive upgrade offer, since the ongoing overage cost frequently exceeds what the upgraded plan's base cost would have been — pointing this out with the customer's actual overage history tends to be more persuasive than a generic upgrade pitch. Downgrades are not subject to the same one-tier limit, since a downgrade reduces the customer's commitment rather than increasing it, but any downgrade should still confirm the customer's current usage comfortably fits within the lower tier's allowance.

title: Customer Account Access Security Overview
content: Account access security rests on three layers: identity verification for phone-based support interactions, password-based authentication for the customer's own self-service login, and internal access controls governing which consultants can view which account details. All three layers are independent — passing one does not substitute for another, so a consultant verifying a caller's identity over the phone does not, for example, grant that caller any change to their online account password without going through the separate password reset process. Consultants themselves are subject to internal access logging identical in spirit to the customer-facing privacy policy: every account lookup a consultant performs is logged and attributable to that consultant, and accessing an account without a legitimate servicing reason is treated the same as a customer-facing privacy violation. Two-factor delivery for sensitive actions defaults to SMS to the phone number on file; if that number is unreachable, escalate to the extended verification path described in the password reset article rather than improvising an alternate delivery channel. Security incidents involving suspected credential compromise (not simple forgotten passwords) should be treated with the same urgency as the fraud detection process, since compromised account access is frequently the first step in a larger fraud attempt rather than an isolated access issue.
